hook: A skateboarder at the bottom of a half-pipe is at a flat spot, and the ramp curves up on both sides. At the lip of a hill the board is also flat, but the ground curves down. Flatness plus the direction of the curve tells you which you have: that is the Second Derivative Test.

ideas: Second Derivative Test: if $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''(c) > 0$, $f$ has a relative minimum at $c$; if $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''(c) < 0$, a relative maximum.
It says nothing when $f''(c) = 0$ or when $f'(c)$ does not exist. Then use the First Derivative Test.
One critical point on an interval, and it is a relative minimum (maximum)? Then it is the absolute minimum (maximum) there, even on an open interval.

misconception.wrong: $f''(c) > 0$, so $f$ has a relative minimum at $c$.
misconception.right: Concave up alone is not a minimum: $f(x) = x^2$ at $x = 1$ is concave up and rising. The test needs a critical point first, $f'(c) = 0$, and then the sign of $f''(c)$. And when $f''(c) = 0$, the test says nothing at all.

summary: At a critical point where $f'(c) = 0$, the sign of $f''(c)$ decides: positive gives a relative minimum, negative a relative maximum, zero gives no conclusion. State both conditions in a justification. With exactly one critical point on an interval, a relative extremum there is absolute.
